claims.text: Accelerated degradation under simultaneous elevated-temperature wear and corrosion is driven by tribocorrosion synergy.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes or disrupts protective oxide or passive films at eutectic interphase boundaries.
Disruption of the protective film exposes vulnerable boundary regions to concentrated localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion undermines interphase-boundary integrity and promotes microcracking.
Corrosion-induced boundary weakening increases subsequent wear.
Mutual reinforcement between film removal, localized corrosion, and wear forms a positive feedback loop that accelerates total degradation.
The initial alloy has intact passive oxide or hardened surface layers associated with its phase boundaries.
Elevated temperature destabilizes or weakens the passive film.
The corrosive environment promotes oxide or passive-film breakdown.
The applied sliding or abrasive wear preferentially affects interphase boundaries.
A comparison among simultaneous tribocorrosion, isolated wear in an inert environment, and isolated corrosion at the same temperature can distinguish coupled degradation from the individual effects.
The combined test will produce approximately 30–50% greater total material loss than the stated baseline.
Both the wear rate and corrosion rate will be higher during simultaneous exposure than during their respective isolated tests.
Combined exposure will produce more severe localized wear penetration at interphase boundaries.
Combined exposure will produce accelerated localized corrosion.
The proposed mechanism requires temperature high enough to compromise film stability and wear severe enough to disrupt the protective film.
The proposed synergy may not occur when temperature, wear, or corrosion severity is insufficient to disturb the passive film.
Tribocorrosion synergy intensity may vary with alloy composition and microstructural features.
Failure of combined exposure to produce a statistically significant excess in overall or interphase-boundary degradation relative to isolated effects would falsify the proposed synergy.
